title: Byung-Chul Han
summary: Byung-Chul Han is a Korean-born philosopher who writes in German, the author of short books about how we live today. His central idea: what weighs on people now is no longer an external prohibition but an inner “you can” — an endless demand to be productive, successful and positive. Hence burnout, depression and the feeling that there is no more time and no more silence.
onEmotions: For Han, many heavy feelings are not only a personal story but also a symptom of an era he calls the “achievement society.” In such a society a person becomes an “entrepreneur of the self” and exploits themselves, and any difficult feeling is treated as an obstacle to efficiency. Han defends the right to negativity: to pain, pause, slowness, to meeting an Other who is truly unlike us. He proposes not to “optimize” feelings but to give them back time and space — through contemplative idleness, ritual, attention to the earth and to another person.

anxiety.text: The anxiety you feel is a real and understandable state, not a sign of weakness. Han would say that today it is often born not from an external threat but from an excess of possibilities. In the “achievement society” there is no strict overseer above us; instead, an endless “you can” sounds within: you can do more, better, faster. If everything is possible, then any failure seems to be only your fault — and anxiety becomes the background of life. Han calls this the “violence of positivity”: pressure that comes not from prohibition but from endless encouragement. Seeing it this way lifts part of the burden. Your anxiety is not proof that you are doing something wrong; it is a natural response to a world with no point of “enough.” You can let yourself see that some of these demands come not from you but from the era.
anxiety.practice: Write down one “I should” that is sounding in your head right now, and ask yourself: whose voice is this — my own, or the voice of the achievement society?

fear.text: Fear is an ancient and honest feeling: it tells you that something matters to you and could be lost. In his late book The Spirit of Hope, Han describes our time as an age saturated with fear: fear of not keeping up, of falling behind, of dropping out of the race, of becoming unneeded. In his view, fear narrows the world — it locks us into survival and makes us cling to the familiar. But Han does not ask us to be ashamed of fear. He sets hope against it — not naive optimism, but openness to what has not yet happened. From this angle one could say: your fear does not have to be defeated by willpower. It is enough to notice that it is not the whole world, and to leave a small window for the possible beside it. Fear and hope can coexist.
fear.practice: Name your fear in one sentence, then add a second line to it: “And yet it is possible that…”

sadness.text: Sadness has a right to exist — even when everyone around you is expected to “stay positive.” Han criticizes what he calls the “palliative society”: a contemporary culture that fears any pain and rushes to numb it right away — with entertainment, a like, a pill, a motivational quote. He calls this fear of pain “algophobia.” For Han, pain and sorrow are a contact with reality, with what does not bend to our will. Without them life becomes smooth, but flat. This view lets you treat sadness not as a breakdown to be fixed urgently but as a form of depth. Sadness slows you down, and in that slowing, what Han values most can appear — attention to the world and to yourself.
sadness.practice: Sit for a couple of minutes without trying to cheer yourself up. Simply ask: what in reality is my sadness touching right now?

grief.text: Grief is the price of having loved. It needs no justification and does not have to pass “on schedule.” Han writes that modernity handles endings badly: our time scatters into separate points, with no rituals to help us say goodbye. In The Disappearance of Rituals he describes rituals as what makes time habitable, the way a house makes space habitable. Mourning was once exactly such a ritual — long, shared, with the right not to hurry anywhere. From Han's point of view one could say: if it seems to you that your grief has “dragged on,” perhaps the problem is not you but a culture that demands you get back in line quickly. Your grief deserves time, form and witnesses.
grief.practice: Invent a small personal ritual of remembrance — light a candle, walk a familiar route, write a few lines — and carry it out without hurrying.

loneliness.text: Loneliness hurts, and the fact that you feel it speaks of a living need for another person. Han notices a paradox: we have never been so “connected” and never suffered so much from loneliness. In The Agony of Eros he describes the “hell of the same”: the digital world mostly shows us reflections of ourselves — similar opinions, similar tastes. The Other disappears — the one who is truly different and can surprise us. Connections multiply while relationships grow thin. This view can bring relief: your loneliness is not proof that something is wrong with you. It is partly produced by the way the time we live in is arranged. And it points a direction — not toward more contacts, but toward one real encounter.
loneliness.practice: Remember a person who once truly surprised you. What exactly about them was “other”?

anger.text: Anger is a legitimate feeling: it often means that something important has been touched. Han draws an interesting distinction. In the book In the Swarm he distinguishes genuine anger from digital outrage — waves of indignation online that flare up quickly and die down just as quickly, changing nothing. Real anger, for Han, can interrupt the usual course of things and open up something new; it requires focus and time. Outrage, by contrast, is scattered and quickly runs out of breath. From this angle one could say: your anger needs neither to be suppressed nor to be vented immediately. It is worth hearing it and letting it ripen — then it can turn from a flash into a clear understanding of what is unacceptable to you and what you want to change.
anger.practice: Before you say or write anything, put it into words: what exactly is my anger protecting? Write it down in one sentence.

shame.text: Shame is one of the most tormenting feelings, and you do not have to hide from it. Han writes about the “transparency society”: today everything must be exhibited, shown, rated. We constantly see ourselves through the eyes of others — through feeds, ratings, comparisons. The power he describes in Psychopolitics does not forbid; it urges us to lay ourselves open. In such a world shame easily becomes chronic: there will always be someone more beautiful, more successful, more productive. From Han's point of view one could say: part of your shame is an effect of constant exposure, not the truth about you. Han defends the right to opacity, to an inner space shown to no one. You have the right not to be fully visible — and in that shelter shame can quiet down.
shame.practice: Notice before whose imagined gaze you feel ashamed right now. Then tell yourself: “This part of my life does not have to be on display.”

guilt.text: Guilt can be heavy, and it speaks of your capacity for responsibility. But Han invites us to look at where guilt that won't let go comes from. In the “achievement society” a person becomes an “entrepreneur of the self”: their own boss and their own worker. They exploit themselves voluntarily — and so they experience any failure as personal guilt rather than as a consequence of circumstances. Han writes that in this situation the exploiter and the exploited coincide. This view does not cancel real responsibility, but it separates it from endless self-accusation. You can ask yourself: did I really act badly — or am I simply failing to meet an impossible standard? In the second case guilt is not the voice of conscience but the voice of the era.
guilt.practice: Write down what you blame yourself for, and note: is it a specific act, or a feeling that you haven't done “enough”?

quote.text: The exploiter is simultaneously the exploited. Perpetrator and victim can no longer be distinguished.
quote.author: Byung-Chul Han

envy.text: Envy is an unpleasant but deeply human feeling, and admitting to it is already honest. Han would explain its power by the structure of the achievement society: each of us is a project to be constantly improved, and digital showcases offer endless material for comparison. We see the polished fragments of other people's lives and compare them with the underside of our own. Han calls this culture “positive”: it has no room for failure, boredom, ordinariness — only successes. From this angle one could say: envy is not a flaw in your character but a predictable effect of a world where everything is put up for comparison. You can accept it as a signal: it points to what you really want — and at the same time to how little we know about other people's lives.
envy.practice: Ask yourself: what exactly do I want from what the other person has — the thing itself, or the recognition that comes with it?

emptiness.text: A feeling of emptiness is hard precisely because it is difficult to explain — but it is real and deserves attention. Han considers depression and apathy characteristic states of our era. In his view, they arise not from lack but from excess: too many stimuli, goals, possibilities — and too little genuine connection with the Other and with the world. A person constantly busy optimizing themselves ends up closed in on themselves, and the world stops responding. Han speaks of the “narcissistic” nature of such emptiness — not in the sense of self-love, but in the sense of losing the outside. This view can help: emptiness is not a verdict on who you are. Perhaps it is saying that what you lack is not new tasks but something external and real that you can simply contemplate.
emptiness.practice: Find one thing near you — a tree outside the window, a cup, a cloud — and for a minute simply look at it, expecting nothing from it.

confusion.text: Feeling lost is natural, especially in a world that changes faster than we can make sense of it. Han writes a great deal about information overload: there is more and more information and less and less understanding. Information, he says, is fragmented and momentary, while knowledge and experience require time, coherence, narrative. In The Crisis of Narration he observes that we have forgotten how to tell the stories that give life meaning and direction. From this angle one could say: your confusion is not a sign of inability but a reasonable response to a flow that has no form. Instead of looking for even more information, you can slow down and try to put what you already know into a story of your own — even an unfinished one.
confusion.practice: Tell yourself the story of the last few months in three or four sentences: “First there was…, then…, now I…”.

fatigue.text: Your tiredness is real, and it is neither laziness nor personal failure. This is Han's central theme. In The Burnout Society he writes that the old disciplinary society rested on prohibitions, while today's “achievement society” rests on a freedom that turns into compulsion: we drive ourselves forward. The result is burnout: a person is exhausted because they endlessly compete with themselves. Han distinguishes a tiredness that isolates from another kind — the one Peter Handke wrote about: a tiredness that lets you let go, stop, and see the world again. This view gives permission: rest is not a reward for achievement but a necessary condition of life. Your tiredness can become not an end but a door to a slower existence.
fatigue.practice: Allow yourself five minutes of doing nothing without the goal of “recharging for work” — simply being tired, without rushing this state.

quote.text: The disciplinary society produces madmen and criminals. Achievement society, in contrast, creates depressives and losers.
quote.author: Byung-Chul Han

boredom.text: Boredom seems like a waste of time, but Han sees something valuable in it. He writes with regret that we have forgotten how to be deeply bored: at the slightest pause we reach for a screen, switch, look for a stimulus. He calls this kind of attention “hyperattention” — scattered, jumping, unable to linger. And yet it is precisely deep boredom, for Han, that is the soil of creativity and contemplation. He refers to Walter Benjamin, for whom boredom hatches experience the way a bird hatches an egg. From this angle your boredom is not a problem demanding an immediate solution but an opportunity. If you don't run from it right away, something new may emerge behind it: a thought, a wish, an image that would not have appeared amid constant busyness.
boredom.practice: When you get bored, wait three minutes before picking up your phone, and notice what comes to mind.

quote.text: Boredom is the dream bird that hatches the egg of experience.
quote.author: Walter Benjamin
quote.source: “The Storyteller” (Han quotes these words in The Burnout Society)

joy.text: Joy is a beautiful feeling, and it needs no justification. Han suggests distinguishing joy from what he calls the cult of positivity. Constant cheerfulness, a “good mood” as a duty, the “like” as a unit of happiness — for him all this is not joy but one more form of pressure. Genuine joy, in his view, is closer to festivity and play: to states that serve nothing, produce nothing and are not built into the logic of usefulness. Han writes about the festival as a time that falls outside the rhythm of work. This view lets you simply be in your joy without turning it into content or into proof of success. Joy doesn't have to be recorded, displayed or justified — it is enough to live it.
joy.practice: Stay with your joy for a minute without photographing it or telling anyone. What changes when it remains yours alone?

love.text: Love and tenderness are among the deepest human experiences. In The Agony of Eros Han writes that love is in danger today because it demands what the achievement society avoids: risk, vulnerability, an encounter with a truly Other. Eros, for Han, is a relation to someone who cannot be reduced to me and my expectations, who cannot be “consumed” or chosen like a product. When love turns into a search for a compatible partner by a list of criteria, it loses its force. From this angle the tenderness you feel is a precious resistance: the capacity to go beyond yourself. Han reminds us that vulnerability in love is not a flaw but its very essence. To love means to let the other remain other.
love.practice: Think of someone you love and name one of their traits you don't fully understand — and let it simply be.

gratitude.text: Gratitude is a quiet and deep feeling that connects you with the world. In Praise of the Earth Han tells how for several years he tended a garden in Berlin. The garden taught him patience, slowness and wonder at what grows beyond our will. The earth, he writes, is a gift, not a resource; we can relate to it with reverence, not only with calculation. From this angle one could say: gratitude is the opposite of the logic of achievement. It acknowledges that much in our lives has been received rather than earned. Such a feeling lightens the load: not everything depends on your efforts, and there is relief in that. Gratitude brings you back to the earth, to what is concrete and alive.
gratitude.practice: Name one thing you received today without earning it — sunlight, someone's gesture, the taste of food.

hope.text: Hope is an important and fragile feeling, and it is good that you have it. In The Spirit of Hope Han distinguishes hope from optimism. Optimism is sure that everything will be fine — it needs neither effort nor risk. Hope, by contrast, is born where there is doubt and darkness; it guarantees no outcome, but it opens up the future. Han sets it against fear, which locks a person into the present and the struggle to survive. Hope, as he sees it, is a movement toward what does not yet exist but is possible. This view lets you not be ashamed of your doubts: your hope does not have to be certainty. It can be quiet and unsure — and still remain a force that carries you forward.
hope.practice: Write down what you hope for, and next to it — one small action that brings it even a little bit closer.

nostalgia.text: Nostalgia is a warm and slightly bitter feeling, and there is nothing shameful in it. Han might explain its power by what he calls the loss of the “scent of time.” In the book of that name he writes that modern time has fallen apart into a string of separate moments, lacking duration and connection. Time used to be filled with rituals, festivals and repetitions that made it habitable. From this angle one could say: in longing for the past, you may be longing not so much for particular events as for a time that had form and rhythm. This insight helps: part of what you remember can be brought back — not as the past itself, but as slowness, a recurring ritual, days that hang together.
nostalgia.practice: Recall what rhythm or ritual there was in the time you miss. Could a small part of it be brought back into your week?

quote.text: From lack of repose our civilization is turning into a new barbarism.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Human, All Too Human (Han quotes these words in The Burnout Society)

craving.text: A sharp “I want it right now” can be very strong, and there is nothing shameful in it. Han would help you look at craving more broadly than as a personal weakness. In Psychopolitics he describes a world that works not through prohibitions but through seduction: everything is arranged to stimulate us, reward us and hold on to us. He calls the smartphone a digital devotional object and the “like” a digital “amen.” From this angle one could say: craving — for the phone, a cigarette, alcohol, anything — often promises a quick release inside a life with no pauses and no point of “enough.” This is neither an excuse nor a verdict, but a way of seeing that you are reaching not only for a substance or a thing, but also for a breather. A wave of desire rises and falls. You can notice it and wait it out without going into battle with it.
craving.practice: When the craving comes, set a timer for three minutes and simply watch it, like the weather: where is it in your body, is it growing or already starting to ebb?

addiction.text: If your life has long been organized around something that is hard to get out of, that is hard — and it is not a moral failure. Han would remind you that addiction doesn't live in a vacuum. In The Burnout Society he writes that the modern person has become an “entrepreneur of the self”: they must constantly work on themselves, raise their efficiency, stay in shape. Han even mentions doping as the logic of the era — the wish to function without stopping. From this angle one could say: a substance or a habit sometimes becomes a way to withstand the pressure, or at least to switch off from it for a while. This doesn't make the cycle any less real, but it removes some of the shame. You are not a “bad person” but a person who found a way to cope — and over time that way became too tight. The way out is rarely a heroic leap; more often it is a slow return of pauses, support and people around you.
addiction.practice: Write one line: “What does this habit free me from, for a while?” If you feel like it, you can talk about this with someone who knows this path from the inside — for example, in a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: The morning after — with a headache, anxiety, gaps in memory and shame — is hard, and you deserve gentleness, not judgment. Han distinguishes the festival from consumption. The festival, as he sees it, is a time that falls outside the rhythm of work, shared and unhurried. Where there is no festival, all that remains is release: a quick “switching off” before a new cycle of effort. From Han's point of view one could say: the moral hangover is also the voice of the achievement society, which in the morning assesses you as a failed project. But you are not a project. In The Palliative Society Han writes that our culture fears pain and hurries to numb it. A hangover is a time when you can choose not to numb, but to slowly come back to yourself: water, quiet, no conclusions about your personality until evening.
hangover.practice: Put off any big conclusions about yourself for today. Do one simple act of care — a glass of water, an open window — and take note of it.

euphoria.text: A burst of euphoria is a vivid experience, and you can simply enjoy it. Han would suggest only one distinction: between an uplift and a race. In the achievement society, he writes, “positivity” reigns — everything is possible, everything is available, nothing stops you. Euphoria sometimes resembles a moment when this “everything is possible” is felt from the inside. Han values a different quality of joy — festive, unhurried, connected with the world and with other people, not only with acceleration. From this angle one could say: to keep what is good in this high, you don't have to turn it immediately into plans, decisions and achievements. You can let it be, like a festival that serves no purpose. Then it will leave behind not only traces of effort but also a memory of lightness.
euphoria.practice: If big plans are being born in this high, write them down — and give yourself a day before deciding anything. For now, simply stay in this feeling.

crash.text: A sharp drop after a high — a celebration, a success, a vivid event — feels like a fall, and that is very understandable. Han writes that the typical illnesses of our time are not “infections” but rather “infarctions”: not a blow from outside, but exhaustion from excess — of stimuli, of effort, of positivity. From this angle one could say: the comedown is not proof that something is wrong with you but the natural flip side of the high. In a world without pauses, everything that flares up brightly must somewhere make up for the strength it spent. Han defends the right to negativity — to moments when you are not at your peak, not productive and not shining. The slump doesn't have to be fixed. It can be lived as a time of quiet, when strength returns slowly, without the demand to get back in shape right away.
crash.practice: Say out loud to yourself: “This is a time of slump, and that's okay.” Choose one very small task for today — and allow yourself to demand nothing more.

panic.text: Panic is frightening: your heart pounds, you can't get enough air, it seems that something irreparable is happening. This is a very hard experience, and you are not alone in it. Han opens The Burnout Society with the idea that every era has its characteristic illnesses, and our age is marked not so much by infections as by the exhaustion of the nervous system — from excess, overload, constant stimulation. From this angle one could say: a wave of panic is not only your personal breakdown but also the body's response to a world with few pauses. Right now, in the middle of the wave, philosophy is not the main thing. The main thing is that such a wave usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. You don't have to fight it; you can lean on what is slow and reliable: the floor, your breath, the things around you.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and make your exhale longer than your inhale. Name out loud five objects you can see around you.

dread.text: Existential dread — “what is it all for,” a sense of the abyss and of finitude — is one of the deepest human experiences, and it does not make you weaker. Han would say that our culture tries to push such questions away. In The Palliative Society he writes that we fear all negativity and strive for a state with neither pain nor mystery — only endless survival and optimization. When meaning is reduced to efficiency, the question “what for?” inevitably rises from within. From this angle one could say: your dread is also a longing for something greater than you, for what cannot be measured by usefulness. Han sees the answer not in quick consolation but in contemplation and connection — with the earth, with another person, with slow time in which life regains its weight.
dread.practice: Step to a window or outside for a minute and look at something alive — a tree, birds, the sky. Don't look for an answer; simply be near something that exists without a purpose.

fomo.text: The feeling that everyone else is living more interesting lives while you are not where you should be is very common and understandable. Han would help you see its source. In the achievement society life itself becomes a project to be optimized, and digital networks turn it into a shop window. Han calls this the “hell of the same”: we see endless variations of the same successful pictures, and each of them says “you could have had more.” From this angle one could say: the fear of missing out is the voice of the endless “you can,” which never says “enough.” But life, for Han, gains depth not from the number of possibilities but from attention to what is already near. The fact that you are not everywhere is not a loss; it is the condition for truly being somewhere.
fomo.practice: Put your phone down and name three things that are in your “here” right now and that are not in anyone else's picture.

sleepless.text: A sleepless night and thoughts at three in the morning are exhausting, and you don't need to blame yourself for them. In The Scent of Time Han writes about the crisis of modern time: it falls apart into a string of moments with no rhythm and no closure. There are no longer thresholds separating work from rest, day from night — everything is open, everything is available, everything goes on. From this angle one could say: night thoughts are the day's unfinished business that found no place of its own. Han values rituals as ways to bring time to a close and give it form. Sleep, in the thought of Walter Benjamin, on whom Han draws, is the high point of bodily rest, and it cannot be seized by effort. You can only prepare a place for it: not solving the day's tasks at night, and letting your thoughts wait until morning.
sleepless.practice: Write down on a sheet of paper everything that is spinning in your head, and add: “This can wait until morning.” Close the notebook the way you close a door.

betrayal.text: Betrayal wounds deeply: what collapses is not only the bond but also your trust in your own ability to trust. This is real pain. In The Transparency Society Han says something subtle about trust: it is only possible between knowing and not knowing. If we knew everything about another person, trust would be unnecessary; we trust precisely because we cannot check everything. From this angle one could say: your trust was not naivety or a mistake. It was a brave step toward an Other who always remains not fully transparent. Betrayal shows how fragile that step is, but it doesn't make it meaningless. Han warns against the temptation of total control. Instead of never opening up to anyone again, you can give yourself time — and acknowledge that the capacity to trust remains your strength.
betrayal.practice: Write one sentence about what your trust says about you — about what you value in relationships.

jealousy.text: Jealousy is a tormenting and deeply human feeling, and you don't need to shame yourself for it. In The Agony of Eros Han writes that love is an encounter with the “atopic” Other: a person who can never be fully put in their place, understood and possessed. This is both the mystery and the risk of love. From this angle one could say: jealousy arises when the otherness of the person you love is felt as a threat — they live their own life, which you cannot fully know or hold on to. That hurts. But Han would warn: the attempt to make the Other fully transparent and your own destroys eros itself. Your jealousy speaks of how much this person means to you. You can acknowledge this fear without turning it into control.
jealousy.practice: Finish the sentence: “What I'm most afraid of losing is…” — and notice what exactly lies behind the jealousy: fear, need, insecurity.

resentment.text: An old grudge is a weight you carry around with you, and it often preserves the memory of a real injustice. Han does not write about resentment specifically, but his thinking about time lets us say something important. In The Scent of Time he distinguishes time that flows and comes to a close from time that gets stuck. A grudge is like a stuck moment: the event is long past but has found no closure. Han values rituals as forms that allow us to close chapters of life. Letting go of a grudge does not mean saying that nothing happened, nor does it necessarily mean forgiving. It means gradually letting what happened take its place in the past, and letting yourself return to the present, where you are more than this wound.
resentment.practice: Write down what exactly hurt you in one honest sentence. Then add: “This story matters, but it is not my whole life.”

heartbreak.text: A broken heart truly hurts, and there is no need to rush this pain. In The Agony of Eros Han defends what he calls the negativity of love. In his view, contemporary culture wants love without risk or vulnerability — “comfortable,” predictable, like a favorable exchange. But real eros, Han writes, is an encounter with the Other that can wound and change us, rather than confirm what we already knew about ourselves. From this angle one could say: your pain is not a sign of failure but evidence that you truly met another person and opened up to them. Han would suggest not “optimizing” grief and not hurrying to turn the page, but giving it time: such a wound is part of the capacity to love.
heartbreak.practice: Allow yourself ten minutes of sadness today without trying to distract yourself: put on music that matches the feeling, and simply stay with it.

impostor.text: The fear that you are about to be exposed is very common, especially among people who work conscientiously. Han would help you see its social side. In the achievement society, he writes, a person is both their own worker and their own overseer: the evaluation never ends, and the bar rises with every success. In The Transparency Society he describes a culture of constant exposure, where everything must be visible and measurable. From this angle one could say: impostor feelings are not proof that you are “not the real thing” but a natural response to a world where no one can ever be “good enough.” If the bar will rise again tomorrow anyway, then today's anxiety says more about the system than about you. You can allow yourself to be a learner rather than flawless.
impostor.practice: Write down three things you really can do — dryly, as facts, without the words “just” or “only.”

self_hatred.text: If your inner voice is merciless toward you, that is very hard, and you deserve gentleness — especially from yourself. That voice does not tell the truth about you. Han describes its origin like this: in the achievement society there is no external master, so a person begins to exploit themselves. They become at once the one who demands and the one from whom it is demanded — and wage war on themselves. From this angle one could say: a harsh inner critic is in large part the internalized voice of an era that is never satisfied. Its verdicts sound like your own, but they are not entirely yours. Han looks for a way out not in even more effort against yourself, but in friendliness, pause and attention to the world around you.
self_hatred.practice: When the critic speaks up, ask: “Would I say this to a friend?” And try saying the same thought in the voice you use with someone close to you.

helplessness.text: Helplessness is a heavy feeling, especially when it seems that nothing depends on you. It deserves compassion. In Psychopolitics Han notices a paradox: in the achievement society a person considers themselves completely free, so they attribute any failure to themselves alone. Instead of seeing the shared conditions, they turn their discontent against themselves — and instead of protest comes exhaustion. From this angle one could say: your powerlessness may partly be an honest knowledge that much really is out of your hands. That is not your fault. Han also defends another kind of strength — the ability to say “no,” to stop, to not take part in the endless race. Sometimes the first step out of helplessness is not a leap but a refusal to demand the impossible of yourself.
helplessness.practice: Divide a sheet of paper into two parts: “what doesn't depend on me” and “one small thing that does.” Choose something from the second column for today.

procrastination.text: “I can't get started” is not laziness or a character defect. Han offers a view that removes some of the shame. In the achievement society, he writes, every task becomes an exam: it must be done well, fast, better than before. When every task is a test of your worth, starting is frightening. Han also speaks of “hyperactivity” and multitasking: attention is scattered among dozens of stimuli, and deep concentration becomes ever harder. From this angle one could say: procrastination can be an overloaded person's protest against the endless “you can.” Han values the ability not to do — as a pause, not as a defeat. Once you allow yourself rest without guilt, it is often easier to take the first small step.
procrastination.practice: Choose the very first micro-action — open the file, write one line — and do only that, giving yourself permission to stop there.

uprooted.text: Being cut off from home — emigration, a move, losing the ground under your feet — affects a person deeply, and your sense of loss is legitimate. Han writes a great deal about losing a foothold. In The Disappearance of Rituals he describes rituals as what makes time habitable, the way a house makes space habitable. In Praise of the Earth he tells of his garden in Berlin: of how tending the soil, the plants and the turning seasons brings back a sense of rootedness. From this angle one could say: home is not only a place on a map but also recurring gestures, rhythms, familiar things. These can gradually be created anew. Not replacing what was lost, but growing new soil beside it — slowly, the way a garden grows.
uprooted.practice: Come up with one small daily ritual — morning tea at the same window, a walk along the same route — and start it today.

overload.text: Overload from an endless stream of news, messages and feeds is real fatigue, not your inability to “cope.” Han writes about this a lot. In In the Swarm he mentions “information fatigue syndrome”: an excess of information doesn't make us smarter but dulls our ability to judge and to discern. He distinguishes hyperattention — rapid switching between stimuli — from deep attention, which is necessary for contemplation and thought. From this angle one could say: your overload is a natural response to a world where the stream never ends. Han proposes not to “manage” the stream better, but sometimes to step out of it. Attention is not an infinite resource, and letting it rest is care, not escape.
overload.practice: For ten minutes put your phone in another room and look out the window. Notice what happens to your attention when nothing is calling it.

unreality.text: The feeling that everything around you, or you yourself, is somehow not real can be unsettling and strange. It deserves gentle treatment. In the book Non-things Han writes about how information displaces things: we touch the dense, weighty world less and less and live more and more among streams of data, screens and images. The world becomes smooth and intangible. From this angle one could say: the experience of unreality resonates with an era in which reality is already losing its weight. This doesn't explain everything, but it can make the feeling less frightening. Han looks for support in things that resist: in soil, in weight, in texture, in slow touch. Sometimes the way back leads through simple sensations of the body and of things.
unreality.practice: Pick up some object — a stone, a cup, a piece of fabric — and for a minute carefully feel it: its weight, its temperature, its roughness.

awe.text: Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious experience, worth savoring to the full. In Saving Beauty Han distinguishes the smooth from the beautiful. The smooth is what pleases instantly, offers no resistance and demands nothing, like a polished screen. The beautiful, for Han, carries something of a wound: it shakes you, stops you, takes you beyond your usual “I.” From this angle one could say: your awe is a moment when the world stops being mere background for your affairs and becomes something greater. It holds the very negativity Han defends — an encounter with what does not belong to you. Such an experience doesn't need to be photographed or explained right away. It is enough to let it hold you still.
awe.practice: Stay one more minute with whatever filled you with awe. Don't film it or describe it — just look or listen.

relief.text: Relief is a warm and well-earned feeling: something heavy has let go. It is worth simply enjoying. Han would suggest seeing a special value in relief — as in a pause. He writes about the Sabbath as a day that exists not to restore strength before new work, but for its own sake: a time in which nothing needs to be produced. In the achievement society relief often turns at once into “now I can get on with the next thing.” From Han's point of view one could say: don't hurry to convert relief into new tasks. This moment is not an empty space between two efforts but a small piece of the good life in itself. You can let it last, like a festival that serves no purpose.
relief.practice: Before taking up the next task, take a few slow breaths in and out and tell yourself: “Nothing is needed right now.”

calm.text: Peace and tranquility are a precious state, and in it you can simply be. For Han this is perhaps one of the most important experiences of all. He defends the vita contemplativa — the contemplative life — setting it against endless activity. In The Burnout Society he recalls Nietzsche's idea of a “pedagogy of seeing”: learning to see means accustoming the eye to calm and patience, letting things come close to us. From this angle one could say: your calm is not idleness or lost time but the return of deep attention, in which the world becomes visible again. It doesn't need to be used for anything. Han would say that it is precisely in such moments that a person stops being a project and becomes simply alive.
calm.practice: Sit still for a minute and notice three sounds around you, without judging them and without changing your posture.

quote.text: Learning to see — accustoming the eye to calmness, to patience, to letting things come up to it.
quote.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
quote.source: Twilight of the Idols (Han quotes these words in The Burnout Society)

inspiration.text: Inspiration is a joyful and lively feeling, and you can meet it with gratitude. Han would help you understand where it comes from. In The Burnout Society he writes that creativity is born of deep attention and even of deep boredom — of a state in which we are not busy with endless switching. Drawing on Benjamin, Han says that without such calm the “dream bird” that hatches experience flies away. From this angle one could say: inspiration is not a result of pressure and self-optimization but a gift of slow, open time. It doesn't have to be turned into a product right away. You can let it live, play, and let the idea unfold while it is not yet obliged to be useful.
inspiration.practice: Write down the idea that came to you by hand, without judging it. Then ask: “What in it do I simply like — with no use at all?”

schadenfreude.text: Schadenfreude is unpleasant to notice in yourself, but a great many people feel it. Han would explain it through the “achievement society”: when everyone becomes an “entrepreneur of the self,” life turns into a nonstop competition, and someone else's success feels like your loss. In such a world another person's failure eases the pressure for a moment: “it's not only me who can't manage.” From Han's point of view one could say: schadenfreude is less a character trait than a symptom of fatigue from endless comparison. Han writes that comparison makes everyone the same and deprives us of a genuine encounter with the Other — a person who is not a rival but simply different. When you notice schadenfreude, you don't have to punish yourself; you can ask where you yourself have grown tired of the race.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: what competition am I taking part in right now without having chosen it? Write down its name.

contempt.text: Contempt arises when someone seems unworthy of our attention. In In the Swarm Han reflects on respect and reminds us that the German Respekt goes back to the Latin respicere — “to look back, to look closely.” Respect, for Han, requires distance: the ability to look at another person without merging with them or appropriating them. The digital environment, he believes, destroys this distance: everything becomes instant, close and public, and instead of respect come waves of disregard. From this angle one could say: contempt is often born of too quick a glance. You are not obliged to respect someone who has caused harm. But you can give yourself time to look more closely — and then contempt will either give way to understanding or become a calm, clear boundary.
contempt.practice: Before passing judgment, look at the situation again, slowly: what might I have missed at first glance?

disgust.text: Disgust is a strong, bodily feeling, and it often has its reasons. In Saving Beauty Han writes that contemporary culture gravitates toward “the smooth”: flawless surfaces, filtered photos, everything that doesn't scratch or resist. Negativity is pushed out of the world — everything uneven, imperfect, truly bodily. From this angle one could say: the smoother our familiar world becomes, the more easily disgust flares up at anything that breaks that smoothness. This doesn't mean your disgust is wrong: sometimes it honestly warns of a boundary that has been crossed. But if it is aimed at yourself or at human imperfection, Han would remind you: what is alive is never smooth. Roughness is a sign of reality, not a flaw.
disgust.practice: Notice what the disgust is aimed at. Ask: is this a warning of danger — or simply something unsmooth, imperfect, alive?

revenge.text: The wish for revenge is a natural response to injustice, and there is nothing shameful in it. In Topology of Violence Han traces how violence changes its form over time: from open clashes to hidden, inner pressure that a person turns against themselves. From this angle one could say: a wish for revenge that cannot and need not be acted on easily turns into endlessly replaying the hurt — that is, into quiet violence against yourself. Han values the contemplative pause — the ability not to respond instantly. Your feeling deserves attention, not execution and not suppression. Beneath it there is often a thirst for recognition: for the pain done to you to be seen. This need can be respected without harming either the other person or yourself.
revenge.practice: Finish the sentence: “What I need most is for someone to acknowledge that…”. Think about whom you could tell this to.

anger_at_loved.text: Anger at the people close to us often comes when there's no strength left — and afterward we feel ashamed. In The Burnout Society Han, drawing on the writer Peter Handke, distinguishes two kinds of tiredness. One is separating: it makes people mute and irritable, locks each person inside themselves, and loved ones suddenly start to seem like an obstacle. The other is a tiredness that trusts the world and brings people closer, as after doing something together. From Han's point of view one could say: anger at loved ones often speaks not of a lack of love but of the exhaustion of someone who has spent all day squeezing results out of themselves. There is no need to take it out on those around you, but there is no need to punish yourself either. It is worth noticing: you need rest, not one more effort.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger at someone close rises, ask yourself: am I angry right now — or just very tired? If it's the second, say so out loud.

ambivalence.text: Loving someone and at the same time not being able to stand them is a hard but deeply human experience. In The Agony of Eros Han criticizes the idea of love as something comfortable and “positive,” free of risk and pain. Such love, he writes, turns into consumption: we want only what is pleasant and convenient from the other. But the real Other, for Han, is always unlike us and resists our expectations — that is their “negativity.” From this angle one could say: your ambivalence is a sign that there is a real person beside you, not a convenient reflection. Irritation and tenderness intertwine because the Other does not submit to you. You don't have to choose one of the feelings: both speak of a living, complicated bond.
ambivalence.practice: Write down one trait of someone close to you that irritates you, and ask: isn't this the very otherness I value them for?

guilty_relief.text: Relief after a breakup, after leaving a job, or after a loved one's long illness can bring guilt with it: how can I feel relieved? Han writes a lot about how the modern person has forgotten how to stop: they live in a mode of endless “more,” where a breather feels like weakness. Caring for someone who is ill, a difficult relationship, an exhausting job all demand strength that is not infinite. Han reminds us of the Sabbath — a day when people stop working not in order to recover for new work but for the sake of rest itself. From his point of view one could say: relief is your body and soul finally receiving the right to pause. It does not cancel the love and care you have given. You can allow yourself this exhale without judging yourself.
guilty_relief.practice: Allow yourself half an hour today of doing nothing and explaining it neither to yourself nor to others. Simply note: I'm allowed to rest.

indifference.text: When something that “should” move you leaves you indifferent, it's easy to get scared for yourself. Han describes an era of excess: an endless stream of information, images, news. In The Burnout Society he speaks of “hyperattention” — a scattered switching among many stimuli in which it is impossible to linger on anything. But a feeling needs time: without it, an impression just slides across the surface. From Han's point of view one could say: your indifference is not necessarily callousness; it may be overload, in which the soul simply stops responding. Han defends deep, contemplative attention — slow and focused. Feeling can come back if you give it silence and time, rather than demanding an immediate “right” reaction from yourself.
indifference.practice: Choose one thing that ought to have moved you, and look at it for five minutes without your phone and without hurry. Demand nothing of yourself.

escape.text: The wish to drop everything and run away — from work, from a city, from a role — often appears when life has turned into one long obligation. Han describes the “achievement-subject,” who believes they are free but in fact exploits themselves: “you can” becomes a compulsion stronger than any order. No wonder you want to leave — although the inner overseer is easy to take along to any city. From Han's point of view one could say: the wish to escape is the voice of the part of you that wants not new productivity but rest, idleness, time that belongs to no one. Han calls this the contemplative life, the vita contemplativa. You don't have to change everything at once. You can start with a small “escape” into unhurriedness — and hear what you really want.
escape.practice: Give yourself a fifteen-minute “escape”: a walk with no goal and no phone. Afterward, write down what you found yourself thinking about.

forbidden_attraction.text: Attraction to someone who is unavailable or seems like “the wrong person” can be unsettling. In The Agony of Eros Han writes that genuine eros is directed at the Other in their otherness — at someone who cannot be possessed, explained or fitted into our schemes. He uses the Greek word atopos — “having no place,” elusive; this is what Socrates' interlocutors called him. Eros, for Han, flares up precisely before the atopic — before what breaks out of the familiar order. From this angle one could say: your attraction speaks not of some corruption in you but of a longing to meet something truly other in a world where everything has become the same and available. It needs neither to be condemned nor to be rushed. You can ask with curiosity: what otherness have I encountered in this person?
forbidden_attraction.practice: Write down what in this person seems truly “other” to you, unlike your familiar world. Simply name it.

social_anxiety.text: Fear of people and of being judged makes any gathering an ordeal. In The Transparency Society Han describes a world where everything must be put on display, rated and compared: every gesture seems to be tested for “likes.” No wonder many people feel as if they are on stage and afraid of making a mistake. From Han's point of view one could say: part of your anxiety is a response to a culture of constant exposure, not only a personal trait. Han defends the right to opacity, to silence, to not being fully visible. In this light, shyness is not a flaw but a way of taking care of your own inner life. You are not obliged to perform or make an impression. You can simply be present, listen, and allow yourself to stay a little closed.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a get-together, tell yourself: “I don't have to be interesting. I can simply be there.” Notice what changes in your body.

uncertainty.text: Uncertainty is exhausting: you want at least some kind of guarantee. In The Spirit of Hope Han distinguishes hope from optimism. Optimism is sure in advance that everything will be fine — it has nothing to overcome. Hope, by contrast, is born where the future is open and guaranteed by nothing: it knows failure is possible and yet turns toward what does not yet exist. Han sets it against fear, which shuts a person up inside themselves. From this angle one could say: uncertainty is not only a source of anxiety but also the very space in which hope is possible at all. If everything were known in advance, there would be nothing to hope for. Instead of trying to guess the future, you can ask yourself: what, in spite of everything, do I hope for?
uncertainty.practice: Finish the sentence: “I don't know what will happen, but I hope that…”. Don't judge whether it is realistic.

waiting.text: Waiting — for an answer, for results, for news — can sometimes wear you out more than the event itself. In The Scent of Time Han writes that modern time has fallen apart into a string of points: we hurry from one event to the next, and everything in between seems empty and lost. Hence the torment of waiting — it drops out of the chain of “useful” moments. Han proposes giving time back its “scent”: learning to linger, to dwell in duration and not only in the result. From this angle one could say: waiting is not necessarily a hole in life. It is also time that can be lived — slowly, with attention to what is near. The answer will come when it comes, and this hour is already yours.
waiting.practice: While you wait, choose one slow action — making tea, looking out the window — and do it twice as slowly as usual.

regret.text: Regret over what you did or didn't do makes you return to the past again and again. In The Crisis of Narration Han writes that today we live among information — scattered facts that quickly go out of date — and are losing the ability to tell stories. Yet it is narrative that ties events into meaning: in a story the past doesn't disappear but becomes part of a path. From Han's point of view one could say: regret is especially painful as long as the mistake remains an isolated fact, an item on an imaginary list of failures. When you write it into the story of your life — with what came before and what came after — it finds its place. A past that has been told stops being a verdict and becomes a chapter.
regret.practice: Write a short story in three sentences: what there was before this choice, what happened, and what came after.

longing.text: Longing for a particular person is the presence of their absence. Han writes that eros is always bound up with distance: the Other is never fully accessible, and it is precisely this unreachability that makes them a living person rather than an object. In a world where everything is instantly within reach — a message, a photo, a call — we have forgotten how to bear absence. From Han's point of view one could say: your longing is not a malfunction but a form of faithfulness to a specific, irreplaceable person. It cannot be filled with a substitute: in the “hell of the same” that Han criticizes, everything is interchangeable, but the person you love is not. You don't have to drive the longing away; you can carry it gently within you as a sign that this person is the only one of their kind for you.
longing.practice: Instead of scrolling through old messages, write down by hand one memory of this person — slowly, with all the details.

world_pain.text: Pain for the world — from news of war, injustice, other people's suffering — can be immense. In The Palliative Society Han describes “algophobia” — a fear of pain that makes contemporary culture try to anesthetize everything and avoid seeing suffering. Against this background your pain is a sign that you have not turned away and that others' suffering touches you. From Han's point of view this is exactly the openness to the Other that is so lacking in a society where everything must be pleasant. But Han also warns about the stream of information that pours down without respite and leaves no room to make sense of anything. From this angle you are not obliged to let the whole stream in. Less news and more silence help your pain remain a human response rather than a stunned numbness.
world_pain.practice: Choose one time of day for the news and don't open it the rest of the time. In the evening, notice how you feel.

rejection.text: Rejection hurts: it feels as if you have been judged as a whole and found unfit. Han describes a “society of positivity” in which relationships increasingly resemble a market: we scroll, rate, “like” and turn people down with a flick of a finger. In this logic a refusal feels like a verdict on your “market value.” From Han's point of view one could say: this is the logic of consumption, not the truth about a person. He writes that a real encounter with the Other is impossible in the mode of choosing a product — it needs time, openness and risk. In this light, rejection is not a verdict on your worth but a sign that the encounter didn't happen. The pain of it is honest and deserves attention. But you are not a profile that failed to make the cut.
rejection.practice: Write down three things about yourself that can't be shown in a questionnaire or profile but that the people close to you know.

abandonment.text: The fear of being abandoned runs very deep: it feels as if your support could vanish at any moment. In The Disappearance of Rituals Han writes that rituals — repeated shared actions — make time habitable, like a home: they give stability and a sense that the world goes on. Today, for Han, there are fewer and fewer rituals; relationships become fluid and noncommittal, and a person has nothing to lean on but their own efforts. From this angle one could say: your fear partly reflects a general lack of stability, not only your personal vulnerability. You can also look for support in small rituals — regular meetings, shared habits, days that belong to you and the people close to you.
abandonment.practice: Come up with one small recurring ritual with someone close — a weekly call, tea together — and suggest it.

unrequited.text: Unrequited love hits hard: the feeling is there, but there is no answer. In The Agony of Eros Han writes that love in its essence is an encounter with an Other who cannot be possessed or disposed of. Contemporary culture, as he sees it, wants love without risk — like a purchase that is guaranteed to pay off. But genuine eros always includes the possibility of getting no answer; that is its “negativity” and its seriousness. From Han's point of view one could say: your love, even unrequited, is evidence that you are capable of going beyond yourself toward the Other — and that, for Han, happens less and less in an age of widespread narcissism. The pain does not devalue the feeling. It was a real movement toward someone.
unrequited.practice: Write yourself one sentence: “I was able to love — and that says about me…”. Finish it the way you feel it.

humiliation.text: Humiliation, especially in front of others, feels like losing the ground under your feet. In In the Swarm Han writes about digital shitstorms that crash down on a person swiftly and impersonally. He notes that there is no respect in them, no distance, no time for understanding. A similar logic works on a smaller scale too: mockery, public judgment, being put on display. From Han's point of view one could say: humiliation often says more about a culture of instant exposure, and about those who humiliate, than about you. Han defends the right to opacity — to an inner space that no one else's gaze can reach. There you remain yourself, however loud the outside noise.
humiliation.practice: Recall a place or a person with whom you are safe from others' judgments. Spend a couple of minutes there, even if only in your mind.

body_shame.text: Dissatisfaction with your body is rarely born on its own — it has cultural roots. In Saving Beauty Han writes that our era worships “the smooth”: polished surfaces, filters, flawless images. In such a culture the body turns into a shop window that must be constantly polished and put on display, and we keep looking at ourselves through the eyes of an imagined viewer, as in an endless selfie. From Han's point of view one could say: your dissatisfaction is largely produced by this gaze, not by an objective truth about you. A living body is never smooth: it has marks, asymmetry, a history. Han believes that beauty is connected precisely with depth and unevenness, not with a flawless surface.
body_shame.practice: Find one “trace of history” on your body — a scar, a small wrinkle, a mole — and remember what stretch of your life it holds.

illness.text: When your body lets you down, fear, fatigue and sometimes anger come, and all of this is understandable. In The Palliative Society Han writes that contemporary culture strives to push pain and illness out of sight: suffering seems a meaningless obstacle to be removed as quickly as possible. So a person who is ill often feels guilty on top of everything, as if they had become “inefficient.” Han argues against this: pain, as he sees it, is part of human experience, not simply a glitch in a mechanism. From this angle one could say: you are not obliged to stay productive and “positive” while ill. You can allow yourself to slow down and accept care from others — this is not weakness but honesty toward your own body.
illness.practice: Tell yourself: “Right now my only task is to be in my body as gently as I can.” You don't need to cancel anything — just take note of it.

pride.text: Pride in what you have done is a healthy, well-deserved feeling. Han notes that in the “achievement society” it strangely struggles to appear: the achievement-subject never reaches the point where they can say “done.” Every success instantly becomes a step toward the next one, and satisfaction slips away. It is precisely this perpetual unfinishedness, for Han, that feeds burnout. From his point of view one could say: healthy pride is a small ritual of completion, a moment when you allow a task to end. Don't rush straight to the next task. Stop, look at what has been done, and let it stand for a while. This is not vanity but an important pause, one our time lacks so badly.
pride.practice: Before taking up the next task, say out loud: “This is done.” Stay with this feeling for a minute.

melancholy.text: Gentle sadness, melancholy, is a quiet feeling that holds depth. Han opens The Agony of Eros with a reflection on Lars von Trier's film Melancholia. He reads the heroine's depression as a closing-in on the self, and the approaching planet as an image of the wholly Other that tears a person out of that enclosure. From Han's point of view one could say: melancholy can cut both ways. It can lock you inside yourself — or, on the contrary, make you sensitive to what lies beyond everyday bustle: fragility, beauty, time slipping away. This gentle sadness is close to the contemplation Han values so highly. It doesn't need to be “fixed” — it can be lived unhurriedly, like an evening with nothing to do.
melancholy.practice: Set aside ten minutes simply to be with this sadness: by a window, with music, on a walk. Don't try to intensify it or to drive it away.
